passage:
A museum showed a repaired pot with visible lines where broken pieces had been joined. The guide said restorers did not hide every crack because the repair itself was part of the object's history.
Students compared the pot with a new copy. The copy looked perfect, but the repaired pot felt more meaningful.
One student said the cracks made it easier to imagine the pot being found, studied, and cared for.
The museum taught that preservation is not always about making old things look new.
A crack can be damage, but it can also be evidence. Repair can honor survival instead of pretending nothing happened.
